before: Obtain cultures, PCR, or viral load before the first dose.
Check baseline BUN, creatinine, and CBC with differential.
Draw baseline LFTs and screen for hepatitis B before hepatitis C therapy.
Confirm pregnancy status and contraception plan before starting.
Review every home drug; these agents carry major CYP interactions.
Weigh the patient and confirm renal dose adjustment with pharmacy.
during: Track creatinine and urine output daily on IV antivirals.
Watch for new tremor, confusion, or hallucinations, especially with renal impairment.
Recheck CBC weekly for neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia.
Monitor LFTs and bilirubin throughout hepatitis B and C therapy.
Check the IV site hourly for infiltration and phlebitis.
hold: Hold and call for rising creatinine or urine output under 30 mL/hr.
Hold and call for new seizure, tremor, or acute confusion.

Report jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, or rising transaminases to the provider promptly, but do not stop a hepatitis B antiviral without an order - abrupt discontinuation of entecavir or tenofovir can trigger a severe acute hepatitis flare (boxed warning).
Hold and call for rash with blistering or mucous membrane involvement.

On nucleoside/nucleotide analogues (NRTIs such as zidovudine, stavudine, didanosine, tenofovir), hold and call for unexplained tachypnea, myalgia, nausea, and fatigue - possible lactic acidosis with hepatic steatosis.
safety: Push fluids to 2 to 3 liters daily unless fluids are restricted.
Infuse IV antivirals on a pump; never give them IV push.
Use chemotherapy gloves for ganciclovir and valganciclovir; do not crush tablets.
Avoid simvastatin and lovastatin with any ritonavir-containing regimen.
Stress finishing the full course; stopping early breeds resistance and flares.
evaluate: Confirm fever, lesions, and viral load fall over the treatment course.
Verify hepatitis C RNA is undetectable 12 weeks after therapy ends.
Check creatinine and CBC return to baseline after IV therapy.
Confirm influenza symptoms shorten and no pneumonia develops.

before: Take baseline BP lying, sitting, and standing plus apical pulse.
Ask about erectile dysfunction drugs before giving any nitrate.
Review baseline creatinine, potassium, and LFTs before starting.
Confirm pregnancy status; several drugs in this class are fetotoxic.
Ask when the last dose was taken and about missed doses.
during: Recheck BP and heart rate 30 to 60 minutes after each dose.
Monitor continuous BP and ECG during any IV vasodilator titration.
Track daily weight and dependent edema for fluid retention.
Ask about headache, dizziness, and palpitations at every check.
Watch for reflex tachycardia after a fast blood pressure drop.
hold: Hold and call for SBP under 90 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold nitrates if sildenafil or vardenafil was taken in the last 24 hours, or tadalafil in the last 48 hours, and notify the provider.
Hold and call for chest pain, syncope, or new dyspnea.
Hold and call for jaundice or ALT above three times normal.
Never stop clonidine or nitrates abruptly; call before any discontinuation.
safety: Change position slowly; orthostatic hypotension causes falls in this class.
Give the first alpha blocker dose at bedtime for first-dose syncope.
Run IV drips on a pump with a second blood pressure source.
Keep the patient seated or lying for sublingual nitroglycerin.
Build in a daily nitrate-free interval to prevent tolerance.
Do not crush extended-release ranolazine or nitrate tablets.
evaluate: Confirm BP reaches the ordered target without symptomatic hypotension.
Verify chest pain episodes and rescue nitroglycerin use decrease.
Check that 6-minute walk distance improves in pulmonary hypertension.
Confirm edema, weight, and exertional dyspnea improve.

before: Ask exactly what happened during any penicillin or cephalosporin reaction.
Draw all ordered cultures before the first dose.
Check baseline creatinine and estimated GFR for renal dosing.
Confirm pregnancy, breastfeeding, and current warfarin or methotrexate use.
Verify patent IV access or the ability to swallow oral doses.
during: Watch the first 30 minutes for hives, wheeze, or throat tightness.
Check the IV site each shift for phlebitis and infiltration.
Track temperature, white count, and the culture and sensitivity result.
Ask daily about new watery diarrhea suggesting Clostridioides difficile.
Recheck creatinine and potassium during prolonged IV therapy.
hold: Stop the infusion and call for hives, wheezing, or facial swelling.
Hold and call for new seizure activity, especially on carbapenems.
Hold and call for three or more watery stools with abdominal pain.
Hold and call for rash with blistering or mucous membrane involvement.
Hold and call for creatinine rising above the ordered parameter.
safety: Keep epinephrine, oxygen, and suction available for the first dose.
Never mix a beta-lactam and an aminoglycoside in the same line.
Flush the line between antibiotics to prevent precipitation.
Teach finishing every dose even after symptoms resolve.
Advise backup contraception; antibiotics can reduce oral contraceptive reliability.
evaluate: Confirm fever, white count, and drainage fall within 48 to 72 hours.
Verify follow-up cultures turn negative.
Check that no rash, C. difficile diarrhea, or yeast superinfection developed.
Confirm the patient completed the full prescribed course.

before: Confirm pregnancy status and last menstrual period before the first dose.
Take a baseline BP, weight, and clot history.
Ask about smoking; smoking over age 35 sharply raises estrogen clot risk.
Review history of breast cancer, stroke, DVT, or liver disease.
Document the baseline bleeding pattern and breast exam.
during: Check BP at every visit; estrogens and androgens raise it.
Ask about calf pain, chest pain, and sudden headache each visit.
Track breakthrough or abnormal vaginal bleeding and report it.
Monitor LFTs and lipids on androgens and oral estrogens.
Watch for edema, weight gain, and breast tenderness.
hold: Hold and call for calf swelling, chest pain, or sudden dyspnea.
Hold and call for sudden vision loss, severe headache, or one-sided weakness.
Hold and call for jaundice or right upper quadrant pain.

Hold and call for a positive pregnancy test on estrogens, androgens/testosterone, and other pregnancy-Category-X hormones. Do not apply this blanket rule to progesterone/progestin therapy prescribed to support a pregnancy - verify the indication with the provider before withholding.
Hold and call for BP above the ordered parameter.
safety: Teach the ACHES warning signs to every estrogen and progestin user.
Plan to stop estrogens 4 to 6 weeks before major elective surgery.
Rotate patch and injection sites on clean, dry, intact skin.
Wash hands before and after inserting vaginal rings, inserts, or gels.
Add backup contraception when antibiotics or enzyme inducers are started.
evaluate: Confirm the target symptom improves: hot flashes, bleeding, or ovulation.
Verify no clot, stroke, or liver injury developed.
Check BP and weight stayed within the ordered range.

before: Confirm hormone receptor status and the treatment goal before starting.
Take baseline BP, weight, lipids, and bone density history.
Draw baseline LFTs, CBC, calcium, and the tumor marker or PSA.
Confirm a negative pregnancy test; these agents cause fetal harm.
Document baseline hot flashes, bone pain, and functional status.
during: Track hot flashes, night sweats, and sleep loss at each visit.
Recheck LFTs and lipids at the scheduled intervals.
Ask about bone pain, joint pain, and new fractures.
Monitor BP, potassium, and edema on androgen-pathway inhibitors.
Watch for calf pain, dyspnea, or vision change from clot.
hold: Hold and call for calf swelling, chest pain, or sudden shortness of breath.
Hold and call for jaundice or ALT/AST above 3 times the upper limit of normal, or above the ordered parameter.
Hold and call for a new seizure or repeated falls.
Hold and call for abnormal vaginal bleeding on antiestrogens.

Report severe flare symptoms in the first weeks of a GnRH agonist (bone pain, urinary obstruction, new back pain or neuro deficits suggesting cord compression) as an emergency; flare is expected and is managed with an antiandrogen, not by withholding the drug.
safety: Push calcium, vitamin D, and weight-bearing exercise for bone protection.
Warn that tumor flare in the first 2 weeks is expected on GnRH agents.
Keep pregnant caregivers from handling crushed or split tablets.
Teach layered clothing and fans for hot flashes; avoid herbal estrogens.
Use pill boxes and alarms; missed doses lower effectiveness.
evaluate: Confirm tumor markers, PSA, or imaging show disease response.
Verify testosterone or estradiol is suppressed to the target level.
Check bone density stayed stable on repeat DEXA.
Confirm hot flashes are tolerable and adherence continued.

before: Take baseline BP sitting and standing before the first dose.
Ask about nitrate use; nitrates with PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated.
Confirm the patient is cardiac-fit for sexual activity.
Document baseline urinary stream, nocturia, and symptom score.
Ask about planned cataract surgery before starting an alpha blocker.
during: Recheck BP after the first dose and after every dose increase.
Ask about dizziness on standing at each visit.
Track urinary frequency, urgency, and nighttime voids.
Watch for priapism, sudden vision loss, or sudden hearing loss.
hold: Hold and call for SBP under 90 or symptomatic dizziness.
Hold and call for an erection over 4 hours; this is an emergency.
Hold and call for sudden vision loss in one eye or hearing loss.
Hold and call for chest pain during or after sexual activity.
Hold all PDE5 inhibitors when any nitrate is given.
safety: Give the first alpha blocker dose at bedtime and rise slowly.
Avoid grapefruit juice and limit alcohol with these drugs.
Tell the eye surgeon about alpha blocker use before cataract surgery.
Keep pregnant women from handling crushed finasteride or dutasteride.
Teach that these drugs do not prevent sexually transmitted infections.
evaluate: Confirm urinary stream, nocturia, and symptom score improve over weeks.
Verify satisfactory erectile function without hypotension or priapism.
Check BP stayed stable with no falls or syncope.
Confirm post-void residual falls on repeat bladder scan.

before: Verify CBC with differential, platelets, creatinine, and LFTs before each cycle.
Confirm dose and body surface area with a second nurse independently.
Confirm antiemetics are ordered; most of these are highly emetogenic.
Confirm a patent, freely flowing IV or central line with blood return.
Verify a negative pregnancy test and document fertility counseling.
during: Check the IV site continuously for burning, swelling, or lost blood return.
Watch the first 15 minutes for flushing, hypotension, or bronchospasm.
Track strict intake, output, and daily weight during hydration.
Recheck CBC at the nadir, usually 7 to 14 days after the dose.
Inspect the mouth daily for mucositis and ulceration.
hold: Hold and call for ANC or platelets below the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for a temperature over 100.4 F during neutropenia.
Hold and call for rising creatinine or urine output under 30 mL/hr.
Stop the infusion for burning, swelling, or leaking at the IV site.
Stop the infusion for hypotension, wheeze, or facial swelling.
safety: Wear double chemotherapy gloves, gown, and eye protection when handling.
Dispose of waste and linens as hazardous for 48 hours after the dose.
Teach flushing the toilet twice with the lid closed for 48 hours.
Keep the extravasation kit and emergency drugs at the bedside.
Teach neutropenic precautions: hand hygiene, no raw foods, avoid sick contacts.
Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor while platelets are low.
evaluate: Confirm tumor response on scheduled imaging or tumor markers.
Verify counts recover before the next cycle starts.
Check nausea was controlled and weight held steady.
Confirm no infection, bleeding, or extravasation injury occurred.

before: Document baseline gait, strength, vision, and relapse history.
Draw baseline CBC with lymphocyte count and LFTs.
Screen for active infection, tuberculosis, and hepatitis B.
Confirm varicella immunity and pregnancy status before immunomodulators.
Give any needed live vaccines before therapy starts, not after.
during: Recheck CBC and LFTs at the intervals ordered for that drug.
Ask each visit about new weakness, vision loss, or cognitive change.
Screen for depression and suicidal thoughts on interferons.
Inspect injection sites for redness, induration, necrosis, and lipoatrophy.
Watch for fever, cough, or urinary symptoms signaling infection.
hold: Hold and call for new focal deficits, aphasia, or personality change.
Hold and call for fever with neutropenia or lymphopenia.
Hold and call for jaundice or transaminases above three times normal.
Hold and call for suicidal ideation or severe depression.
Hold and call for a positive pregnancy test.
safety: Rotate subcutaneous sites and let the syringe reach room temperature first.
Apply ice before and after injection to reduce site reactions.
Use inactivated vaccines only during therapy; avoid live vaccines.
Assess fall risk; keep assistive devices and pathways clear.
Plan rest periods and cooling strategies for heat-triggered fatigue.
evaluate: Confirm relapse rate and MRI lesion count fall over time.
Verify walking speed, strength, and independence hold or improve.
Check labs stayed in range and no serious infection occurred.

before: Collect sputum for smear, culture, and susceptibility before the first dose.
Draw baseline LFTs, bilirubin, creatinine, CBC, and uric acid.
Document baseline visual acuity and red-green color vision.
Ask about alcohol use, hepatitis history, and HIV status.
Review every home drug; rifamycins induce many drug metabolisms.
during: Check LFTs monthly and with any symptom of hepatitis.
Collect monthly sputum cultures until two consecutive results are negative.
Ask monthly about numbness, tingling, and vision change.
Confirm adherence each visit; directly observed therapy is preferred.
Watch for rash, fever, and joint pain.
hold: Hold and call for jaundice, dark urine, or anorexia with nausea.
Hold and call for ALT above three times normal with symptoms.
Hold and call for blurred vision or lost red-green discrimination.
Report new numbness or burning in the feet promptly; expect pyridoxine (B6) to be added or increased. Do not stop TB therapy on your own - the provider decides whether any drug is held.
Hold and call for a QTc above the ordered parameter on bedaquiline.
safety: Give on an empty stomach when tolerated; food lowers rifampin absorption.
Keep the patient in airborne isolation with N95 use until cleared.
Warn that rifamycins turn urine, sweat, and tears orange-red.
Add backup contraception; rifamycins make hormonal contraceptives fail.
Avoid alcohol completely; it multiplies hepatotoxicity risk.
Never take one drug alone; single-drug therapy breeds resistance.
evaluate: Confirm sputum cultures convert to negative by 2 to 3 months.
Verify cough, night sweats, fever, and weight loss resolve.
Check LFTs and vision stayed normal through therapy.
Confirm the full 6 to 9 month course was completed.

before: Screen for recent surgery, active bleeding, and prior hemorrhagic stroke.
Confirm symptom onset time and that the treatment window is open.
Draw CBC, platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, and type and screen first.
Start two large-bore IVs and draw all labs before the dose.
Record baseline neuro exam, BP, and weight in kilograms.
during: Check vital signs and neuro status every 15 minutes during the infusion and for the first 2 hours from the start, then every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly through 24 hours. Report any neuro decline, severe headache, nausea/vomiting, or an acute BP rise immediately and stop the infusion.
Watch IV sites, gums, urine, and stool for bleeding.
Monitor continuous ECG for reperfusion dysrhythmias.
Assess for sudden headache, vomiting, or decreased consciousness.
Recheck hemoglobin and platelets after the infusion.
hold: Stop the infusion for sudden severe headache, vomiting, or new deficit.
Stop the infusion for any uncontrolled or suspected internal bleeding.

For IV alteplase/tenecteplase in acute ischemic stroke, do not give and call if BP is above 185/110; BP must be lowered and kept under 180/105 after the bolus. For other thrombolytic indications, follow the ordered/protocol BP limits (severe uncontrolled hypertension, generally over 180/110, is a contraindication).
Stop the infusion for anaphylaxis, angioedema, or tongue swelling.
safety: Avoid IM injections, arterial sticks, and catheter insertion for 24 hours.

After thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke, give no anticoagulant or antiplatelet for 24 hours (until follow-up imaging). For STEMI and other indications, antithrombotics are often ordered concurrently - follow the specific order set.

Use compressible upper-extremity sites, apply pressure to arterial puncture sites for at least 30 minutes, then apply a pressure dressing and monitor the site closely; avoid internal jugular and subclavian punctures and all IM injections.
Keep bed rest and the head of bed per the stroke protocol.
Keep type and crossmatched blood available during and after therapy.
Use a dedicated line; give no other drugs through it.
evaluate: Confirm chest pain resolves and ST segments return toward baseline.
Verify neuro deficits improve on serial NIH Stroke Scale checks.
Check no intracranial or major bleeding occurred within 24 hours.
Confirm perfusion returns: pulses, warmth, and reperfusion dysrhythmias.

before: Check baseline potassium, sodium, magnesium, creatinine, and BUN.
Take BP sitting and standing plus apical pulse before each dose.
Weigh the patient and record baseline edema and lung sounds.
Ask about sulfonamide allergy and current digoxin or lithium use.
Make sure a toilet, urinal, or bedside commode is within reach.
during: Weigh daily at the same time in the same clothing.
Record strict intake and output every shift.
Recheck potassium and magnesium; hypokalemia triggers dysrhythmias.
Assess lung sounds, edema, and jugular venous distention daily.
Ask about muscle cramps, weakness, tinnitus, and dizziness.
hold: Hold and call for potassium under 3.5 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for SBP under 90 or symptomatic orthostatic hypotension.
Hold and call for new tinnitus or hearing loss.
Hold and call for urine under 30 mL/hr with a rising creatinine.
Hold and call for weight loss faster than the ordered daily goal.
safety: Give the daily dose early so diuresis does not disrupt sleep.
Push IV doses slowly; rapid administration causes permanent hearing loss.
Have the patient rise slowly; use a gait belt for ambulation.
Encourage potassium-rich foods unless potassium is restricted.
Warn about photosensitivity; use sunscreen and protective clothing.
evaluate: Confirm weight drops and edema, crackles, and dyspnea improve.
Verify urine output rises within 1 hour of an oral dose.
Check potassium and creatinine stayed within range.
Confirm BP reached target without dizziness or falls.

before: Inspect and measure the lesion; note size, color, drainage, and borders.
Photograph or chart a baseline description so change is measurable.
Ask about allergy to the drug, preservatives, lanolin, and latex.
Confirm pregnancy status before any retinoid or systemic-absorption agent.
Check whether skin at the site is broken, weeping, or already infected.
during: Remeasure the lesion weekly and chart redness, scaling, and drainage.
Watch the application site for burning, worsening rash, or new pustules.
Watch for spreading warmth, purulent drainage, and fever signaling secondary infection.
Inspect for skin thinning, striae, and telangiectasia on potent topical steroids.
Ask about itching relief and whether the patient is sleeping through the night.
hold: Hold and call for blistering rash, mucous membrane lesions, or fever.
Hold and call if the treated area becomes purulent, warm, or spreading.
Hold and call for a positive pregnancy test on any retinoid.

Report new hyperglycemia, moon face, or edema on long-term potent topical steroids; these suggest systemic absorption and HPA suppression. Do not stop abruptly — the provider tapers the potency, amount, or frequency.
Hold and call for facial or airway swelling after application.
safety: Wear gloves, apply a thin film, and wash hands before and after.
Keep potent steroids off the face, axillae, and groin unless specifically ordered.
Do not cover with plastic or occlusive dressing unless ordered; occlusion raises absorption.
Apply to clean dry skin; keep all products out of the eyes.
Use sunscreen and protective clothing with retinoids and other photosensitizing agents.
evaluate: Confirm lesion size, erythema, and pruritus decrease over the ordered course.
Confirm skin stays intact with no new atrophy, striae, or infection.
Confirm the patient sleeps without scratching and reports less discomfort.

before: Document baseline seizure type, frequency, duration, and any aura.
Draw baseline CBC, LFTs, and electrolytes including sodium.
Screen for suicidal ideation; every drug in this class raises that risk.
Confirm pregnancy status and contraception plan; most are teratogenic.
Review all home drugs for enzyme induction, including oral contraceptives.
during: Inspect the skin daily for new rash during the first 8 weeks.
Draw serum levels as trough samples just before the next dose.
Reassess mood and suicidal thinking at every contact.
Check gait, nystagmus, diplopia, and slurred speech as early toxicity signs.
Recheck CBC and LFTs on the ordered schedule.
hold: Hold and call for any new rash; it may be Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Report suicidal statements or an abrupt mood change to the provider immediately and institute suicide precautions, but continue the antiseizure drug on schedule unless the provider orders otherwise - abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus.
Hold and call for jaundice, dark urine, or rising transaminases.

Report fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, bruising, or a falling white count immediately (carbamazepine, valproate, felbamate, phenytoin) and hold the next dose only on provider order - never stop an antiseizure drug abruptly.
Never stop abruptly; sudden withdrawal triggers status epilepticus.
safety: Keep suction, oxygen, and an airway at the bedside; keep the bed low.
Institute seizure precautions and never put anything in the mouth during a seizure.
Give with food to reduce nausea unless the drug requires an empty stomach.
Warn against driving and machinery until sedation and dizziness resolve.
Advise a backup contraception method with enzyme-inducing agents.
evaluate: Confirm seizure frequency and duration fall from the documented baseline.
Verify serum levels sit within the ordered therapeutic range.
Confirm the patient is alert enough for school, work, and self-care.
Confirm no rash, no bruising, and stable liver and blood counts.

before: Send fungal cultures, KOH prep, or blood cultures before the first dose.
Draw baseline LFTs, BUN, creatinine, potassium, and magnesium for systemic therapy.
Review every home drug; azoles are strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
Obtain a baseline ECG when other QT-prolonging drugs are ordered.
Inspect and document the treatment site or lesion appearance.
during: Recheck LFTs and creatinine at least weekly during systemic therapy.
Monitor potassium and magnesium and replace before they bottom out.
Watch the monitor for QT prolongation on azoles.
Take a temperature every 4 hours; fever should trend down.
Inspect the IV site each shift for phlebitis and infiltration.
hold: Hold and call for jaundice, dark urine, or transaminases greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal (hepatotoxicity is mainly an azole and amphotericin concern; echinocandins are much lower risk).
Hold and call for QTc prolongation or new ventricular ectopy.
On amphotericin B (and other renally cleared systemic antifungals), hold and call for a rising creatinine or urine output under 30 mL/hr; most azoles and echinocandins do not require this.
Hold and call for rash with blistering or mucous membrane involvement.
On amphotericin B, check K+ and Mg2+ before each dose; report hypokalemia and expect replacement before the infusion. This is not a routine hold parameter for azoles or echinocandins.
safety: Infuse systemic antifungals on a pump; never give them IV push.
Verify the exact amphotericin product and dose with a second nurse.
Separate oral azoles from antacids, PPIs, and H2 blockers, which block absorption.
Teach that therapy runs weeks to months and stopping early causes relapse.
Check topical versus systemic route on the order before applying or infusing.
evaluate: Confirm fever, white count, and repeat cultures normalize.
Confirm lesions, thrush plaques, or vaginal discharge resolve.
Verify LFTs, creatinine, and electrolytes return to baseline.

before: Rate pain 0 to 10 with location, quality, and what worsens it.
Count respirations for a full minute and record a baseline sedation score.
Take blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygen saturation before the first dose.
Verify the last dose time and total opioid taken in 24 hours.
Screen for sleep apnea, COPD, head injury, and the current bowel pattern.
during: Recheck respirations and sedation 15 to 30 minutes after IV, 1 hour after oral.
Use a sedation scale; rising sedation comes before respiratory depression.
Reassess the pain score at peak effect and chart the number.
Track bowel movements daily and start the ordered bowel regimen with dose one.
Check for bladder distention and urinary retention each shift.
hold: Hold and call for a respiratory rate under 12 or a rising sedation score.
Hold and call for oxygen saturation under 90 percent or new apnea.
Hold and call for systolic BP under 90 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold and call if the patient cannot be roused to answer a question.
Hold and call for no bowel movement in 3 days with abdominal distention.
safety: Keep naloxone and a bag-valve mask at the bedside.
Verify dose and pump settings with a second nurse; these are high-alert drugs.
On PCA, only the patient presses the button; teach the family never to push it.
Keep the bed low with the call light in reach and assist the first ambulation.
Never crush or chew extended-release tablets; dose dumping is fatal.
Avoid benzodiazepines and alcohol; combined CNS depression stops breathing.
evaluate: Confirm the pain score falls to the patient's stated goal.
Confirm respirations stay 12 or above with adequate oxygen saturation.
Confirm the patient can move, cough, deep breathe, and sleep.
Confirm bowels move without straining.

before: Draw baseline calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and vitamin D levels.
Check creatinine; most bisphosphonates are avoided with poor renal function.
Arrange a dental exam before IV bisphosphonates or denosumab.
Document the baseline DEXA T-score and any prior fracture.
Correct hypocalcemia before giving any bone-resorption inhibitor.
during: Recheck serum calcium after the first dose and on the ordered schedule.
Check Chvostek and Trousseau signs and ask about perioral tingling and cramps.
Ask about new thigh or groin pain suggesting an atypical femur fracture.
Ask about jaw pain, loose teeth, or a nonhealing socket at every visit.
Ask about heartburn and painful swallowing on oral bisphosphonates.
hold: Correct hypocalcemia BEFORE giving a bisphosphonate or denosumab and hold those drugs until calcium and vitamin D are replete. Calcium and vitamin D supplements are not held for a low calcium.
Hold and call for new dysphagia, retrosternal pain, or hematemesis.
Hold and call for jaw pain or exposed bone in the mouth.
Hold and call for creatinine clearance below the drug's cutoff.
Hold and call for calcium above normal on vitamin D analogs.
safety: Take oral bisphosphonates first thing with 8 ounces of plain water only.
Keep the patient fully upright and NPO for the required post-dose interval.

Give oral bisphosphonates with plain water on an empty stomach and stay upright: nothing else by mouth - no food, drink, calcium, antacids, or iron - for at least 30 minutes for alendronate and risedronate, and at least 60 minutes for ibandronate.
Give the ordered calcium and vitamin D unless serum calcium is high.
Remove throw rugs and add grab bars; these patients fracture easily.
evaluate: Confirm the follow-up DEXA T-score is stable or improved.
Confirm serum calcium and phosphorus stay in normal range.
Confirm no new fractures and less bone pain.

before: Take blood pressure and heart rate sitting and standing before the first dose.
Confirm the patient is not pregnant; these drugs injure the fetal kidney.
Draw baseline potassium, BUN, and creatinine.
Ask about prior angioedema on an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
Verify no ACE inhibitor or aliskiren is also ordered.
during: Recheck blood pressure before each dose and 1 to 2 hours after.
Recheck potassium and creatinine 1 to 2 weeks after starting or titrating.
Watch for lip, tongue, or facial swelling and any voice change.
Weigh daily and check lower-leg edema in heart failure patients.
Ask about dizziness on standing, especially in the first week.
hold: Hold and call for systolic BP under 90 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for potassium above 5.5 mEq/L.
Hold and call for creatinine rising more than 30 percent above baseline.
Hold and call for any facial or airway swelling; the drug is stopped permanently.
Hold and call for a positive pregnancy test.
safety: Have the patient sit at the bedside before standing; first-dose hypotension causes falls.
Avoid salt substitutes and potassium supplements; they raise potassium fast.
Avoid NSAIDs; they blunt the effect and raise creatinine.
Give at the same time daily and never stop abruptly for feeling well.
Teach home blood pressure logging with the cuff on a bare upper arm.
evaluate: Confirm blood pressure reaches the ordered goal.
Confirm potassium and creatinine stay stable on repeat labs.
Confirm less dyspnea, edema, and weight gain in heart failure.

before: Document the baseline pain pattern, timing, and what relieves it.
Check for black tarry stool, coffee-ground emesis, and baseline hemoglobin.
Confirm pregnancy status before misoprostol.
Review home drugs; acid suppression changes absorption of many of them.
Draw baseline magnesium when long-term PPI therapy is planned.
during: Track pain relief and how many rescue antacid doses the patient uses.
Watch for new watery diarrhea; C. difficile risk rises on PPIs.
Recheck magnesium and B12 on PPI therapy past 1 year.
Check stools for occult blood and follow hemoglobin during ulcer treatment.
hold: Hold and call for watery diarrhea with fever or abdominal pain.

Report black tarry stool, hematemesis, or a falling hemoglobin to the provider immediately and anticipate IV PPI therapy, NPO status, type and screen, and urgent endoscopy; do not withhold the acid suppressant on your own.
Hold and call for a positive pregnancy test on misoprostol.
Hold and call for muscle cramps, tetany, or magnesium below normal.
safety: Give PPIs 30 to 60 minutes before the first meal of the day.
Do not crush delayed-release capsules; open and sprinkle on applesauce if allowed.
Separate antacids from other oral drugs by at least 1 to 2 hours.
Reinforce that PPI courses are time limited, not automatically lifelong.
Teach smoking cessation and alcohol limits; both delay ulcer healing.
evaluate: Confirm heartburn and epigastric pain resolve.
Confirm stools stay guaiac negative and hemoglobin holds steady.
Confirm follow-up endoscopy shows the ulcer or esophagitis healed.

before: Document baseline mood, sleep, appetite, and energy in the patient's words.
Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, a plan, means, and prior attempts.
Review all drugs for serotonergic overlap: triptans, tramadol, linezolid, St. John's wort.
Confirm at least 14 days since any MAOI was stopped.
Draw a baseline sodium in older adults; SSRIs cause hyponatremia.
during: Assess suicidal thinking at every contact: weekly for the first 4 weeks, every 2 weeks for weeks 5 to 8, then at 12 weeks and as clinically indicated — and after every dose change.
Watch for agitation, tremor, clonus, diaphoresis, and fever: serotonin syndrome.
Track sleep, appetite, and energy; energy returns before mood lifts.
Recheck sodium 2 to 4 weeks after starting in older adults.
Ask about bruising, nosebleeds, and dark stools, especially with NSAIDs.
hold: Hold and call for new or worsening suicidal thoughts or self-harm plans.
Hold and call for fever, rigidity, clonus, and agitation.
Hold and call for sodium below normal with headache or confusion.
Hold and call for a switch to mania: no sleep, racing speech, grandiosity.
Never stop abruptly; taper to avoid discontinuation syndrome.
safety: Arrange removal of firearms and stockpiled medication during the first weeks.
Give in the morning if the drug causes insomnia, at bedtime if it sedates.
Warn that full effect takes 4 to 6 weeks even though side effects start now.
Avoid alcohol and St. John's wort entirely.
Name the sexual side effects up front; surprise is why patients stop the drug.
evaluate: Confirm mood, sleep, and appetite improve by 4 to 6 weeks.
Confirm the patient denies suicidal thoughts on direct questioning.
Confirm sodium and weight stay stable.
Confirm the patient returns to work, school, or usual activity.

before: Document baseline voiding pattern: frequency, urgency, leakage, and nocturia.
Bladder scan for post-void residual before the first dose.
Send a urinalysis; treat infection before treating the bladder.
Screen for narrow-angle glaucoma, gastric retention, and chronic constipation.
Take a baseline blood pressure and heart rate.
during: Recheck post-void residual and ask about trouble starting the stream.
Keep a voiding diary of urgency episodes and leaks per day.
Watch for new confusion, hallucinations, or memory change in older adults.
Recheck blood pressure and heart rate at each follow-up.
Ask about constipation and dry mouth at every visit.
hold: On antimuscarinic bladder drugs (oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin) or mirabegron, hold and call for urinary retention or a rising post-void residual; on bethanechol or an alpha-blocker given for retention, report the residual but do not hold - retention is the reason the drug is ordered.
Hold and call for new confusion, hallucinations, or a fall.
Hold and call for eye pain, halos, and blurred vision: angle-closure glaucoma.
Hold and call for blood pressure above the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for no bowel movement in 3 days with abdominal distention.
safety: Keep the call light in reach and a clear lit path to the bathroom.
Do not crush or chew extended-release tablets.
Offer sugar-free gum, ice chips, and frequent oral care for dry mouth.
Add fiber and fluid; anticholinergic constipation can reach impaction.
Warn about overheating; these drugs reduce sweating in hot weather.
evaluate: Confirm urgency episodes, leaks, and nocturia drop from the diary baseline.
Confirm post-void residual stays low and the patient empties comfortably.
Confirm no new confusion, falls, or constipation.

before: Draw cultures before the first dose.
Ask about prior tendon rupture, myasthenia gravis, and aortic aneurysm.
Review for QT-prolonging drugs and check baseline potassium and magnesium.
Check creatinine for renal dose adjustment.
Ask about seizure history; this class lowers the seizure threshold.
during: Ask daily about new tendon pain, especially at the Achilles.
Ask about numbness, tingling, or burning in the hands and feet.
Check blood glucose; these drugs cause both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia.
Watch the monitor for QT prolongation.
Watch for confusion, agitation, and hallucinations in older adults.
hold: Hold and call for tendon pain, swelling, or a pop; rest the limb immediately.
Hold and call for new numbness or weakness in an extremity.
Hold and call for sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain: aortic dissection.
Hold and call for confusion, agitation, or seizure activity.
Hold and call for watery diarrhea; C. difficile is common with this class.
safety: Separate fluoroquinolones from antacids, calcium, iron, zinc, multivitamins, and sucralfate: ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after, moxifloxacin at least 4 hours before or 8 hours after.
Infuse IV doses over at least 60 minutes; rapid infusion drops blood pressure.
Use sunscreen and cover up; photosensitivity reactions are severe.
Push fluids to 2 to 3 liters daily to prevent crystalluria unless restricted.
Check INR closely with warfarin; fluoroquinolones raise it.
Avoid in children and pregnancy unless no alternative exists.
evaluate: Confirm fever, white count, and repeat cultures normalize.
Confirm the infected site improves and the patient finishes the full course.
Confirm tendons, nerves, and mental status remain normal.

before: Chart the baseline bowel pattern: last stool, frequency, consistency, and effort.
Auscultate bowel sounds and palpate for distention before any laxative.
Rule out obstruction, impaction, and acute abdomen before giving a laxative.
Ask about fever, blood in stool, and recent antibiotics before treating diarrhea.
Draw baseline potassium, sodium, and creatinine before repeated laxative or antidiarrheal use.
during: Record every stool: number, consistency, color, and any blood or mucus.
Track daily weight, intake, and output while diarrhea continues.
Recheck potassium and magnesium during prolonged laxative use or ongoing diarrhea.
Watch for worsening distention, absent bowel sounds, and vomiting.
Rate abdominal pain and cramping before and after each dose.
hold: Hold and call for abdominal rigidity, rebound tenderness, or absent bowel sounds.
Hold and call for bloody stool, fever, or suspected C. difficile before any antidiarrheal.
Hold and call for hypokalemia below the ordered parameter or a new dysrhythmia.
Hold and call if no stool passes and distention worsens after a laxative.
Hold and call for severe abdominal pain with rectal bleeding; ischemic colitis.
safety: Give laxatives with a full glass of water and push fluids all day.
Keep the call light and a clear path to the commode; urgency causes falls.
Avoid daily long-term stimulant laxatives; dependence and hypokalemia follow.
Separate bulk laxatives and binders from other oral drugs by 2 hours.
Refrigerate biologic solutions and mix gently; never shake, and inspect for particles.
evaluate: Confirm a soft formed stool without straining within the expected time frame.
Confirm stool frequency falls and consistency firms on antidiarrheal therapy.
Confirm abdominal cramping and distention decrease.
Confirm potassium, sodium, and weight stay stable.

before: Confirm the drug, toxin, or deficiency being treated and the time of exposure.
Draw the level that guides therapy: acetaminophen, digoxin, iron, INR, or vitamin.
Ask about allergy, including egg, fish, shellfish, and prior antidote reactions.
Establish IV access and record baseline vital signs before any IV antidote.
Verify the weight-based dose and concentration against the order before drawing it up.
during: Take vital signs every 5 to 15 minutes during IV administration.
Watch for flushing, urticaria, wheezing, and hypotension signaling anaphylaxis.
Recheck the guiding lab after the dose: level, INR, ammonia, or oxygen saturation.
Watch for return of the original toxicity as the antidote wears off.
Inspect the IV site for infiltration and phlebitis during infusion.
hold: Stop the infusion and call for wheezing, facial swelling, or falling blood pressure.
Stop and call for rash, itching, or fever developing during the infusion.
Hold and call if the label, dose, or concentration does not match the order.

Report seizure activity during or after administration immediately. Stop the drug and call for a flumazenil-associated seizure - but do NOT withhold antidotes such as pyridoxine (isoniazid overdose), atropine/pralidoxime, glucose, or calcium, where a seizure usually signals undertreated poisoning. Get provider direction before holding any antidote.
safety: Keep epinephrine, oxygen, and a bag valve mask at the bedside for IV antidotes.
Monitor longer than the antidote half-life; many toxins outlast the reversal.
Infuse continuous antidotes on a pump with the line clearly labeled.
Protect light-sensitive vitamins and antidotes from light during infusion.
Stay with the patient during and right after the first dose.
evaluate: Confirm the target lab corrects: level falls, INR drops, or the deficiency resolves.
Confirm toxicity reverses: level of consciousness, respirations, rhythm, or bleeding improve.
Confirm no rebound toxicity after the antidote is stopped.

before: Screen suicide risk directly: ideation, plan, means, and prior attempts.
Record baseline mood, sleep, appetite, and weight.
Take sitting and standing blood pressure and pulse.
List every serotonergic drug, MAOI, triptan, tramadol, and St. John's wort.
Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting another antidepressant, and 14 days after most antidepressants before an MAOI - but 5 weeks after fluoxetine.
during: Reassess suicidal thinking weekly for the first month, especially as energy returns.
Recheck blood pressure at each visit and after every dose increase.
Watch for serotonin syndrome: fever, agitation, clonus, rigidity, and diarrhea.
Track weight, appetite, and sleep at every follow-up.
Ask about dry mouth, constipation, and sexual side effects that drive nonadherence.
hold: Hold and call for new or worsening suicidal thoughts, agitation, or hostility.
Hold and call for serotonin syndrome: hyperthermia, clonus, rigidity, and confusion.
Hold and call for seizure activity or syncope.
Hold and call for blood pressure above the ordered parameter.
Hold and call for a widened QRS, QT prolongation, or new dysrhythmia.
safety: Never stop abruptly; taper to prevent dizziness and flu-like discontinuation symptoms.
Tell the patient mood lifts in 4 to 6 weeks; energy returns before mood.
Dispense limited quantities while suicide risk is present; TCA overdose is lethal.
Rise slowly from bed; orthostatic hypotension causes falls in older adults.
Give sedating drugs at bedtime and activating drugs in the morning.
evaluate: Confirm mood, sleep, appetite, and interest improve by 4 to 6 weeks.
Confirm the patient denies suicidal thoughts and can state a crisis plan.
Confirm blood pressure and weight stay within the ordered range.

before: Screen for coronary disease, stroke, and uncontrolled hypertension before a triptan or ergot.
Record baseline blood pressure and pulse.
Chart the headache pattern: frequency, severity, aura, triggers, and acute drug days.
List all serotonergic drugs; SSRIs and SNRIs raise serotonin syndrome risk.
Ask when the headache started; abortive drugs work best at the first sign.
during: Rate pain 0 to 10 before the dose and again 1 to 2 hours after.
Watch for chest, jaw, neck, or throat tightness after a triptan or ergot.
Recheck blood pressure after dosing; triptans and CGRP blockers raise it.
Watch for serotonin syndrome: agitation, clonus, fever, and diarrhea.
Count headache days and doses per month to catch medication overuse.
hold: Hold and call for chest pressure, arm pain, or dyspnea after a dose.
Hold and call for a sudden worst-ever headache, fever, or neck stiffness.
Hold and call for numbness, weakness, or speech change; no triptans in hemiplegic migraine.
Hold and call for cold, blue, or painful hands and feet on an ergot.
Hold and call for blood pressure above the ordered parameter.
safety: Give at the first sign of migraine; do not wait for severe pain.
Do not give a triptan and an ergot within 24 hours of each other.
Limit acute drugs to about 2 days a week to prevent rebound headache.
Darken the room, cut noise, and let the patient rest after the dose.
Hold driving after any dose that causes dizziness or sedation.
evaluate: Confirm pain drops to mild or none within 2 hours of the abortive dose.
Confirm nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia resolve.
Confirm monthly migraine days fall on preventive therapy.

before: Chart baseline nausea severity, number of emesis episodes, and triggers.
Check hydration: mucous membranes, skin turgor, urine output, and orthostatic vitals.
Draw potassium, sodium, and magnesium when vomiting has been prolonged.
Review the ECG and QTc before 5-HT3 antagonists and phenothiazines.
Ask about Parkinson disease and past dystonic reactions before dopamine blockers.
during: Count emesis episodes and measure emesis and urine output each shift.
Watch for extrapyramidal signs: restlessness, stiff neck, tongue protrusion, eye rolling.
Watch for oversedation and a falling respiratory rate.
Recheck orthostatic blood pressure before ambulating.
Track intake, output, and daily weight until vomiting stops.
hold: Hold and call for acute dystonia, oculogyric crisis, or new tremor and rigidity.
Hold and call for fever with rigidity and altered mental status; neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Hold and call for QTc prolongation or a new dysrhythmia.
Hold and call for blood or coffee-ground emesis.
Hold and call if sedation keeps the patient from protecting the airway.
safety: Keep diphenhydramine available to treat a dystonic reaction from dopamine blockers.
Give the dose before chemotherapy or the trigger, not after vomiting starts.
Raise the head of bed 30 to 45 degrees to reduce aspiration risk.
Assist with ambulation; sedation and orthostatic hypotension cause falls.
Offer ice chips, oral care, and small sips once vomiting stops.
evaluate: Confirm vomiting stops and the patient keeps oral fluids down.
Confirm the nausea rating falls and the patient eats.
Confirm urine output, weight, and electrolytes return to baseline.

before: Record baseline weight, blood pressure, pulse, and intake and output.
Draw baseline potassium, sodium, BUN, creatinine, and glucose.
Ask about sulfa allergy before thiazides and acetazolamide.
List potassium supplements, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and salt substitutes.
Check for digoxin; hypokalemia from a thiazide triggers digoxin toxicity.
during: Weigh daily at the same time, same scale, same clothing.
Recheck potassium and sodium within a week of starting or changing the dose.
Take orthostatic blood pressure; dizziness on standing signals volume loss.
Compare urine output to intake every shift.
Watch for muscle cramps, weakness, and irregular pulse from potassium shifts.
hold: Hold and call for potassium above 5.0 mEq/L on any potassium-sparing agent.
Hold and call for potassium below 3.5 mEq/L on a thiazide.
Hold and call for systolic BP under 90 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for rising creatinine or urine output under 30 mL/hour.
Hold and call for palpitations, marked weakness, or new ECG changes.
safety: Give in the morning so diuresis does not interrupt sleep.
Assist to the bathroom and keep the path clear; urgency causes falls.
Teach potassium-rich foods on thiazides and no salt substitutes on potassium-sparers.
Use sunscreen; thiazides and sulfonamides cause photosensitivity.
Rise from lying to sitting to standing slowly to prevent syncope.
evaluate: Confirm weight falls and dependent edema decreases as ordered.
Confirm blood pressure reaches the ordered goal.
Confirm potassium, sodium, and creatinine stay in range.
Confirm breathing eases and lung sounds clear.

before: Confirm travel history, exposure, and the parasite identified or suspected.
Ask about G6PD deficiency before primaquine and tafenoquine.
Draw baseline CBC, LFTs, and creatinine.
Get a baseline ECG and potassium before chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, and pentamidine.
Document baseline vision and arrange a retinal exam for long-term therapy.
during: Recheck CBC for hemolysis and cytopenias during therapy.
Watch for dark urine, jaundice, and back pain signaling hemolysis.
Watch the ECG for QT prolongation on chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, and pentamidine.
Ask about tinnitus, blurred vision, and trouble reading at every visit.
Track the fever curve and repeat blood smears as ordered.
hold: Hold and call for dark urine or a falling hemoglobin; hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Hold and call for new visual field loss, blurred vision, or trouble reading.
Hold and call for QTc prolongation, syncope, or a new dysrhythmia.
Hold and call for hallucinations, severe anxiety, or depression on mefloquine.
Hold and call for a blistering rash or mucous membrane lesions.
safety: Give with food or milk to cut nausea unless the drug specifies otherwise.
Give prophylaxis on schedule before, during, and after travel as ordered.
Store antimalarials locked away; a small overdose kills a child.
Separate from antacids and kaolin by at least 4 hours; they block absorption.
Continue mosquito precautions: nets, repellent, and covered skin.
evaluate: Confirm fever resolves and blood smears clear as ordered.
Confirm diarrhea and stool studies clear for the treated organism.
Confirm hemoglobin, LFTs, and vision stay stable.

before: Take an apical pulse for a full minute before every dose.
Take blood pressure before every dose and compare to the ordered parameters.
Ask about asthma, COPD, heart block, and decompensated heart failure.
Check for diabetes; beta blockers mask the tachycardia and tremor of hypoglycemia.
Weigh the patient and auscultate lungs for baseline heart failure signs.
during: Recheck apical pulse and blood pressure before each dose and after every increase.
Watch for new dyspnea, crackles, weight gain, and edema.
Monitor the ECG for bradycardia and new heart block during IV therapy.
Have diabetic patients check glucose more often; warning signs are blunted.
Ask about fatigue, dizziness, depression, and cold hands and feet.
hold: Hold and call the provider for apical HR under 60.
Hold and call for systolic BP under 90 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for new wheezing or bronchospasm.
Hold and call for new crackles, weight gain over 2 to 3 pounds in a day, or worsening dyspnea.
Hold and call for second- or third-degree heart block on the monitor.
safety: Never stop abruptly; rebound tachycardia, hypertension, angina, and MI follow.
Rise slowly; orthostatic hypotension and dizziness cause falls.
Keep the patient on continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring during IV therapy.
Keep dosing times consistent and give with food when the order says so.
Teach the patient to take and record a daily radial pulse at home.
evaluate: Confirm blood pressure and heart rate reach the ordered goals.
Confirm angina episodes and nitroglycerin use decrease.
Confirm heart failure signs improve: less dyspnea, stable weight, less edema.

before: Draw the electrolyte being treated before dosing: potassium, magnesium, phosphate, or bicarbonate.
Confirm urine output is adequate before giving potassium or magnesium.
Record baseline blood pressure, pulse, respirations, and cardiac rhythm.
Check renal function; kidney disease changes every electrolyte dose.
Review the ECG for peaked T waves, flattened T waves, or a widened QRS.
during: Recheck the target electrolyte after each dose or on the ordered schedule.
Watch the cardiac monitor for rhythm change during IV potassium or magnesium.
Check deep tendon reflexes and respiratory rate during magnesium infusion.
Track intake, output, and bowel pattern; binders cause constipation.
Inspect the IV site hourly during potassium infusion for pain and burning.
hold: Hold and call for urine output under 30 mL/hour before giving potassium.
Hold and call for absent deep tendon reflexes or respirations under 12 on magnesium.

Hold potassium (and other electrolyte) supplements and call immediately for a widened QRS, peaked T waves, or new dysrhythmia. Do NOT hold potassium binders for these findings — they are the treatment for hyperkalemia; give them and call for emergency measures.
Hold and call for absent bowel sounds or suspected obstruction before a binder.
Stop the infusion and call for burning or infiltration at the potassium site.
safety: Never give potassium chloride IV push; always dilute and run on a pump.
Keep peripheral IV potassium at or below 10 mEq per hour on a general floor.
Keep calcium gluconate at the bedside as the antidote during magnesium infusion.

Separate binders from other oral drugs per the specific product - at least 3 hours before or after for patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, and check the label for phosphate binders and sevelamer; 2 hours is not sufficient for all of them.
Give oral potassium with food and a full glass of water or juice.
evaluate: Confirm the target level returns to normal range on the follow-up lab.
Confirm ECG changes resolve and the rhythm stays stable.
Confirm muscle strength, reflexes, and mental status return to baseline.

before: Confirm the airway is secured or intubation equipment and a provider are ready.
Confirm sedation and analgesia are ordered and infusing before any paralytic.
Record baseline vital signs, oxygen saturation, and continuous ECG.
Draw baseline potassium; note burns, crush injury, and prolonged immobility.
Ask about malignant hyperthermia in the patient and the family.
during: Monitor continuous ECG, pulse oximetry, capnography, and blood pressure.
Check train-of-four with a nerve stimulator to titrate the paralytic.
Watch for rising heart rate, blood pressure, and tearing; these signal pain or awareness.
Check ventilator alarms, settings, and breath sounds every hour.
Watch for rigidity, rising end-tidal CO2, and fever; malignant hyperthermia.
hold: Hold the paralytic and call if sedation and analgesia are not running.
Hold and call for hyperkalemia or a rhythm change after succinylcholine.

Stop the agent and call for ANY sign of malignant hyperthermia - an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2, unexplained tachycardia, masseter or generalized muscle rigidity. Do not wait for fever; hyperthermia is a late sign. Get the MH cart and dantrolene and call for help immediately.
Hold and call for systolic BP under 90 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold and call if the airway or ventilator cannot be secured immediately.
safety: Never give a neuromuscular blocker without an airway and ventilator at hand.
Tape the eyes closed and use lubricant; the blink reflex is gone.
Reposition every 2 hours and use pressure-injury prevention; the patient cannot move.
Store paralytics separately with warning labels; these are high-alert look-alike risks.
Apply sequential compression devices and give the ordered DVT prophylaxis.
evaluate: Confirm train-of-four matches the ordered depth of block.
Confirm the patient synchronizes with the ventilator and oxygenation improves.
Confirm full strength returns after reversal: sustained head lift, grip, and tidal volume.

before: Draw baseline CBC with differential, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelet count.
Check baseline iron studies: ferritin, transferrin saturation, and serum iron.
Take baseline blood pressure; uncontrolled hypertension must be treated before an ESA.
Ask about prior reactions to IV iron, factor products, or growth factors.
Confirm the ordered hemoglobin or platelet target; these drugs are not dosed to normal.
during: Recheck CBC on the ordered schedule to track hemoglobin, ANC, and platelets.
Take vital signs before, 15 minutes into, and at the end of every infusion.
Watch for flushing, wheezing, back pain, and hypotension during infusion; anaphylaxis.
Watch for chest pain, dyspnea, leg swelling, or slurred speech; thrombosis.
Ask about left upper quadrant or left shoulder pain on growth factors; splenic rupture.
hold: Hold the ESA and call when hemoglobin exceeds the ordered target or climbs rapidly.
Stop the infusion and call for urticaria, wheezing, hypotension, or facial swelling.
Hold and call for blood pressure above the ordered parameter or uncontrolled hypertension.
Hold and call for a new seizure, stroke symptoms, or suspected DVT or PE.
Hold and call for sudden left upper quadrant pain radiating to the shoulder.
safety: Keep epinephrine, oxygen, and resuscitation equipment at the bedside for IV iron and factors.
Infuse IV iron at the ordered rate; rapid infusion causes hypotension and flushing.
Roll reconstituted factor and biologic vials gently; never shake, and inspect for particles.
Refrigerate ESAs and growth factors; do not freeze and do not use if frozen.
Rotate subcutaneous sites and document them; avoid bruised, scarred, or edematous skin.
Assist with ambulation while hemoglobin is low; orthostatic dizziness causes falls.
evaluate: Confirm hemoglobin rises toward the ordered target without overshooting it.
Confirm ANC recovers and febrile episodes decrease on colony-stimulating factors.
Confirm platelet count rises into the ordered range with no thrombosis.
Confirm fatigue, pallor, and exertional dyspnea improve.
Confirm bleeding stops and joint swelling resolves after factor replacement.

before: Draw a baseline fasting lipid panel: LDL, HDL, triglycerides, total cholesterol.
Draw baseline ALT and AST before starting a statin, fibrate, or niacin.
Ask about unexplained muscle pain, weakness, or prior statin intolerance.
Confirm the patient is not pregnant or breastfeeding before a statin.
Review the med list for gemfibrozil, amiodarone, and azole antifungals; myopathy risk.
during: Recheck the lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks after starting or changing a dose.
Ask at every contact about muscle pain, tenderness, weakness, and dark urine.
Draw CK when muscle pain appears; rhabdomyolysis raises it sharply.
Recheck liver enzymes for jaundice, dark urine, or right upper quadrant pain.
Check fasting glucose and A1C; statins raise blood glucose slightly.
hold: Hold and call for muscle pain and weakness with dark tea-colored urine.
Hold and call for CK far above baseline; rhabdomyolysis.
Hold and call for jaundice or liver enzymes above the ordered threshold.
Stop the statin and call immediately if the patient becomes pregnant.
Hold and call for severe epigastric pain radiating to the back; pancreatitis.
safety: Give simvastatin, lovastatin, and fluvastatin in the evening; cholesterol synthesis peaks at night.
Avoid grapefruit juice with simvastatin, lovastatin, and atorvastatin.
Separate bile acid sequestrants from other drugs: 1 hour before or 4 hours after.
Mix powdered sequestrants in 4 to 6 ounces of fluid; never swallow dry.
Have the patient sit up when taking sequestrants; push fluids and fiber for constipation.
evaluate: Confirm LDL falls to the ordered goal on the follow-up panel.
Confirm triglycerides fall on fibrate, niacin, or omega-3 therapy.
Confirm liver enzymes and CK stay within normal limits.
Confirm the patient reports no muscle pain or weakness.

before: Document baseline mental status, orientation, gait, strength, and muscle tone.
Take baseline blood pressure and apical pulse lying and standing.
Draw baseline liver enzymes; several of these drugs are hepatotoxic.
Review the med list for opioids, benzodiazepines, and alcohol use.
Ask about seizures, recent falls, and difficulty swallowing.
during: Check sedation and dizziness before every transfer and ambulation.
Recheck orthostatic blood pressure after each dose increase.
Compare spasticity, tremor, or cognitive scores against the documented baseline.
Recheck liver enzymes on the ordered schedule for tizanidine, dantrolene, and riluzole.
Watch for bradycardia, drooling, cramping, and diarrhea on cholinesterase inhibitors.
hold: Hold and call for apical HR under 60 on a cholinesterase inhibitor.
Hold and call for SBP under 90 or symptomatic orthostatic hypotension.
Hold and call for jaundice, dark urine, or liver enzymes above the ordered threshold.
Hold and call for oversedation, new confusion, or a fall.
Hold and call for muscle rigidity with fever and altered mental status.
safety: Never stop baclofen abruptly; withdrawal causes high fever, rigidity, and seizures.
Keep the bed low, the call light close, and assist with all transfers.
Give sedating muscle relaxants at bedtime when the schedule allows.
Give rivastigmine and galantamine with food to limit nausea and vomiting.
Check intrathecal baclofen pump alarms and refill dates; pump failure is an emergency.
evaluate: Confirm spasticity and painful spasms decrease without new weakness.
Confirm cognitive and functional scores hold steady or decline more slowly.
Confirm involuntary movements decrease on the AIMS score.
Confirm muscle strength, ptosis, and swallowing improve on pyridostigmine.
Confirm no falls, oversedation, or new confusion.

before: Verify the order, dose, body surface area, and cumulative dose with a second nurse.
Confirm CBC with differential, ANC, platelets, creatinine, and liver function are acceptable.
Confirm baseline LVEF or echo before any anthracycline dose.
Verify a patent central line or a new, freely flowing peripheral IV with blood return.
Confirm the ordered premedications are given: antiemetics, steroids, antihistamines.
during: Check the IV site every 5 to 10 minutes for burning, swelling, and blood return.
Take vital signs during the first 30 minutes; hypersensitivity reactions peak early.
Watch for dyspnea, flushing, hypotension, and back pain during infusion.
Assess numbness, tingling, foot drop, and reflexes before each cycle; neuropathy.
Check temperature and ANC daily; fever during neutropenia is an emergency.
hold: Stop the infusion immediately for burning, swelling, or loss of blood return; extravasation.
Stop and call for dyspnea, urticaria, hypotension, or facial swelling.
Hold and call for ANC or platelets below the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for a new S3, crackles, edema, or a drop in LVEF.
Hold and call for a temperature of 100.4 F or higher during neutropenia.
safety: Wear double chemotherapy gloves, gown, and eye protection with a closed-system transfer device.
Keep the extravasation kit and the ordered antidote at the bedside.
Never give a vinca alkaloid intrathecally; intrathecal administration is fatal.
Handle urine, stool, vomit, and linens as hazardous for 48 hours after the dose.
Start neutropenic precautions: hand hygiene, no fresh flowers, screen visitors for illness.
Use a soft toothbrush and avoid rectal temperatures and suppositories.
evaluate: Confirm tumor markers, imaging, or measurable disease show response.
Confirm counts recover before the next scheduled cycle.
Confirm nausea and vomiting stay controlled on the antiemetic regimen.
Confirm the IV site stays intact with no extravasation injury.
Confirm no new neuropathy, mucositis, or cardiac symptoms develop.

before: Take baseline blood pressure sitting and standing, apical pulse, and weight.
Draw baseline potassium, BUN, and creatinine.
Ask about angioedema on any prior ACE inhibitor; that history is a contraindication.
Confirm the patient is not pregnant; ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic in every trimester.
Review the med list for potassium supplements, spironolactone, ARBs, and NSAIDs.
during: Recheck blood pressure 1 hour after the first dose; first-dose hypotension is common.
Recheck potassium and creatinine within 1 to 2 weeks of starting or increasing.
Ask daily about a dry, persistent, nonproductive cough.
Check for swelling of lips, tongue, face, or new hoarseness; angioedema.
Check sodium and potassium on the hydrochlorothiazide combinations; the thiazide lowers both.
hold: Hold and call for SBP under 90 or per the ordered parameters.
Stop the drug and call rapid response for lip, tongue, or throat swelling.
Hold and call for potassium above 5.5 mEq/L or per the ordered parameter.
Hold and call for creatinine rising sharply above baseline.
Hold and call immediately for a positive pregnancy test.
safety: Have the patient sit or lie for the first dose and 1 hour after.
Rise slowly from lying to sitting to standing; orthostatic dizziness causes falls.
Avoid salt substitutes; most are potassium chloride.
Avoid NSAIDs; they blunt the effect and worsen kidney injury.
Give the thiazide combination products in the morning to limit nighttime urination.
evaluate: Confirm blood pressure reaches the ordered goal.
Confirm edema, weight, and dyspnea improve in heart failure.
Confirm potassium and creatinine stay within the ordered range.
Confirm the cough is tolerable or the provider switches to an ARB.

before: Draw baseline CBC, platelet count, PT/INR, aPTT, and creatinine.
Ask about active bleeding, recent surgery, stroke, and peptic ulcer disease.
Ask about prior heparin-induced thrombocytopenia before any heparin product.
Confirm an accurate weight in kilograms; most doses are weight based.
Review the med list for aspirin, NSAIDs, antiplatelets, SSRIs, and herbals.
during: Inspect gums, stool, urine, IV sites, and skin for bleeding every shift.
Recheck platelet count; a drop over 50 percent suggests HIT.
Watch for sudden headache, confusion, or unequal pupils; intracranial bleed.
Track hemoglobin and hematocrit for a slow fall; occult bleeding.
Check for back pain, leg weakness, or incontinence after neuraxial anesthesia; spinal hematoma.
hold: Hold and call for active bleeding: hematemesis, melena, or frank hematuria.
Hold and call for platelets below the ordered parameter or a 50 percent drop.
Hold and call for lab values above the ordered therapeutic range.
Hold and call for a new severe headache, vision change, or altered mental status.
Hold before invasive procedures for the provider's ordered hold time.
safety: Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor; no flossing hard and no straight razors.
Hold pressure on injection and venipuncture sites for at least 5 minutes.
Do not aspirate or massage subcutaneous sites; rotate sites and leave the bruise alone.
Have a second nurse independently verify IV heparin concentration, dose, and pump settings.
Post fall precautions; a head strike on an anticoagulant can bleed into the brain.
Do not stop an oral anticoagulant abruptly without an order; rebound clotting follows.
evaluate: Confirm INR, aPTT, or anti-Xa sits in the ordered therapeutic range.
Confirm no new bruising, bleeding, or fall in hemoglobin.
Confirm clot symptoms improve: less leg pain, swelling, and dyspnea.
Confirm platelet count stays stable.

before: Draw baseline CBC with platelet count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit.
Ask about active bleeding, prior stroke or TIA, and peptic ulcer disease.
Confirm the ordered stop date before surgery; most need 5 to 7 days.
Review the med list for aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants, and herbal supplements.
Take baseline blood pressure and heart rate before starting an IV agent.
during: Inspect gums, stool, urine, and puncture sites for bleeding every shift.
Recheck platelet count within hours on IV agents; acute profound thrombocytopenia occurs.
Watch the femoral sheath site for hematoma, swelling, and pulse changes after PCI.
Watch for sudden headache, one-sided weakness, or slurred speech; intracranial bleed.
Track hemoglobin for a slow drop; occult GI bleeding.
hold: Hold and call for active bleeding from any site.
Hold and call for platelets below the ordered parameter.
Hold and call for a new severe headache or focal neurologic change.
Hold and call before any urgent invasive procedure until the provider confirms timing.
Hold and call for SBP under 90 with chest pain on an IV agent.
safety: Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor; hold pressure on all puncture sites.
Keep the leg straight and the head of bed low while a femoral sheath is in.
Avoid IM injections during glycoprotein IIb/IIIa infusions.
Give oral antiplatelets with food to reduce GI upset.
Post fall precautions; head injury bleeds more on antiplatelets.
evaluate: Confirm no chest pain, stent thrombosis, or new ischemic symptoms.
Confirm walking distance improves on cilostazol or pentoxifylline.
Confirm platelet count and hemoglobin stay stable.
Confirm no bruising, bleeding, or unexplained drop in blood pressure.

before: Confirm volume status is corrected; vasopressors cannot fix hypovolemia.
Verify a central line, or the largest reliable vein as a short-term bridge.
Record baseline blood pressure, MAP, heart rate, rhythm, and urine output.
Confirm the ordered MAP target and the titration parameters.
Draw baseline potassium, magnesium, and lactate.
during: Check blood pressure every 5 to 15 minutes while titrating; arterial line preferred.
Keep continuous ECG monitoring; watch for tachycardia, ectopy, and new dysrhythmias.
Check the IV site hourly for blanching, coolness, pain, and swelling.
Track hourly urine output; report output under 0.5 mL/kg/hr.
Check capillary refill, pulses, and skin color and temperature every hour.
hold: Stop the infusion and call for blanching, pain, or swelling at the site; extravasation.
Titrate down and call for chest pain, new ST changes, or ventricular dysrhythmias.
Call for heart rate above the ordered parameter or new atrial fibrillation.
Titrate down and call for MAP above the ordered target.
Call for dusky, cold, painful fingers or toes; digital ischemia.
safety: Give through a central line whenever possible; peripheral use is a temporary bridge.
Never bolus or flush a vasopressor line; a bolus causes a hypertensive crisis.
Use a dedicated smart pump channel and label the line at the pump and the patient.
Keep phentolamine available per policy for vasoconstrictor extravasation.
Wean down in the ordered increments; abrupt stopping drops the pressure suddenly.
Have a second nurse verify the concentration and pump settings at every handoff.
evaluate: Confirm MAP holds at or above the ordered target, commonly 65 mmHg.
Confirm urine output rises above 0.5 mL/kg/hr.
Confirm lactate falls and capillary refill shortens.
Confirm mentation improves and the skin warms.
Confirm the dose can be weaned down over time.

before: Draw baseline A1C, fasting glucose, creatinine, and eGFR.
Take baseline blood pressure sitting and standing and record volume status.
Ask about recurrent urinary tract infections and genital yeast infections.
Ask about type 1 diabetes, prior DKA, and current insulin or sulfonylurea doses.
Inspect the feet and document any ulcer, blister, or poor perfusion.
during: Check blood glucose on the ordered schedule; hypoglycemia rises with insulin or sulfonylureas.
Recheck creatinine and eGFR after starting and with any acute illness.
Ask about dysuria, urgency, and genital itching or discharge each visit.
Watch for nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and deep rapid breathing; euglycemic DKA.
Check orthostatic blood pressure and daily weight for volume depletion.
hold: Hold and call for nausea, vomiting, and rapid breathing even with normal glucose.
Hold and call for perineal pain, redness, swelling, and fever; Fournier gangrene.
Hold and call for SBP under 90 or symptomatic dehydration.
Hold and call when eGFR falls below the ordered threshold.
Hold during acute illness, fasting, or before surgery per the ordered plan.
safety: Give once daily in the morning before the first meal.
Push fluids unless restricted; dehydration drives most of the adverse effects.
Perform perineal hygiene after voiding; glucose in urine feeds yeast.
Inspect the feet daily and report any new blister, ulcer, or redness.
Rise slowly; osmotic diuresis causes orthostatic dizziness and falls.
evaluate: Confirm A1C and fasting glucose fall toward the ordered goal.
Confirm blood pressure and weight fall modestly without dehydration.
Confirm heart failure symptoms and hospitalizations decrease.
Confirm no genital infection, DKA, or rise in creatinine.

before: Draw baseline creatinine and BUN and calculate creatinine clearance.
Document baseline hearing, tinnitus, and balance before the first dose.
Obtain ordered cultures before the first dose.
Confirm the dosing weight and the ordered peak and trough draw times.
Ask about myasthenia gravis or other neuromuscular disease; blockade risk.
during: Draw the trough within 30 minutes before the next dose and the peak 30 minutes after infusion.
Track intake, output, and daily weight; report urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/hr.
Recheck creatinine and BUN every 2 to 3 days during therapy.
Ask daily about ringing, fullness in the ears, vertigo, and new hearing loss.
Watch for muscle weakness and shallow breathing; neuromuscular blockade.
hold: Hold and call for a trough above the ordered range; toxicity is trough driven.
Hold and call for creatinine rising above baseline or falling urine output.
Hold and call for new tinnitus, hearing loss, or vertigo.
Hold and call for new muscle weakness or respiratory depression.
Hold and call for rash, fever, or other hypersensitivity signs.
safety: Infuse IV doses over 30 to 60 minutes; never give IV push.
Push fluids unless restricted; hydration protects the kidneys.
Do not mix aminoglycosides and penicillins in the same line; they inactivate each other.
Avoid other nephrotoxins: NSAIDs, vancomycin, loop diuretics, and contrast dye.
Label level tubes with the exact draw time and the last dose time.
evaluate: Confirm fever, white count, and infection signs resolve.
Confirm peak and trough levels sit in the ordered range.
Confirm creatinine and urine output stay at baseline.
Confirm hearing and balance are unchanged from baseline.

before: Confirm the full combination regimen; a single antiretroviral alone breeds resistance.
Draw baseline CD4 count, viral load, CBC, liver enzymes, and creatinine.
Screen for hepatitis B; stopping some agents triggers a severe hepatitis flare.
Review every prescription, OTC, and herbal product; interactions are extensive.
Ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding before the first dose.
during: Recheck viral load and CD4 count on the ordered schedule.
Track ALT, AST, and bilirubin for hepatotoxicity.
Watch for fever with rash, malaise, and GI upset in the first six weeks.
Watch for unexplained tachypnea, muscle pain, and fatigue; lactic acidosis.
Ask about mood changes and suicidal thoughts at every contact.
Watch for new fever and swollen nodes weeks in; immune reconstitution syndrome.
hold: Stop and call for any rash with fever, blistering, or mucosal lesions.
Hold and call for ALT or AST above the ordered threshold, or jaundice.

Report new suicidal ideation, severe depression, or psychosis immediately (most often efavirenz, rilpivirine, dolutegravir) and expect a regimen change; do not interrupt antiretroviral therapy without a provider order, as interruption promotes resistance.
Hold and call for unexplained tachypnea, severe abdominal pain, or rising lactate.
Hold and call for creatinine rising above the ordered parameter.
safety: Give doses at the same times daily; missed doses drive resistance.
Check each drug's food rule; some need food, some need an empty stomach.
Separate antacids, calcium, iron, and multivitamins from integrase inhibitors per the ordered interval.
Verify renal dosing before giving tenofovir- or lamivudine-containing products.
Teach that therapy lowers transmission risk but does not replace barrier protection.
Never skip doses during illness; call the provider instead of stopping.
evaluate: Confirm viral load falls to undetectable within the expected months.
Confirm CD4 count rises and no opportunistic infection develops.
Confirm the patient can state how many doses were missed this month.
Confirm weight is stable and energy improves.

before: Take baseline weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, and pulse.
Draw baseline fasting glucose, A1C, and a lipid panel.
Obtain a baseline ECG plus potassium and magnesium; many prolong the QT interval.
Record a baseline AIMS score for abnormal involuntary movements.
Ask about seizures, Parkinson disease, and dementia; boxed mortality warning applies.
during: Watch for fever, rigidity, altered mental status, and unstable vitals; neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Check each shift for tremor, masked face, restlessness, and neck or jaw spasm.
Repeat the AIMS on the ordered schedule for tardive dyskinesia.
Recheck weight, fasting glucose, and lipids at the ordered intervals.
Take lying and standing blood pressures during titration.
Ask daily about suicidal thoughts and new agitation.
hold: Stop and call for fever with rigidity and rising CPK; this is an emergency.
Hold and call for acute dystonia: neck torsion, jaw spasm, or upward eye deviation.
Hold and call for SBP under 90 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for QTc above the ordered threshold, syncope, or palpitations.
Hold and call for a new seizure or ANC below the ordered threshold.
safety: Assist with ambulation and have the patient rise slowly; sedation and orthostasis cause falls.
Give IM doses deep into the ventrogluteal site; never give a depot injection IV.
Check the mouth after oral doses when nonadherence is suspected.
Teach sun protection and heat precautions; these drugs impair temperature regulation.
Warn against alcohol and other CNS depressants; sedation is additive.
Push fluids and offer sugar-free candy for anticholinergic dry mouth.
evaluate: Confirm hallucinations, delusions, and agitation decrease over the first weeks.
Confirm the patient sleeps, eats, and takes part in self-care.
Confirm the AIMS score stays at baseline with no new involuntary movements.
Confirm weight, glucose, and lipids stay within the ordered limits.

before: Screen for active infection and latent TB before starting a biologic.
Verify immunizations are current; no live vaccines during therapy.
Ask about IgA deficiency and prior reactions to immune globulin products.
Draw baseline CBC, liver enzymes, and creatinine.
Confirm the product, strength, and route; these names look alike.
during: Take vital signs before, during, and after every infusion per policy.
Watch for flushing, chills, back pain, dyspnea, and hypotension; infusion reaction.
Watch for headache with fever and stiff neck after IVIG; aseptic meningitis.
Track creatinine and urine output after immune globulin infusions.
Ask about new fever, cough, night sweats, and wounds that will not heal.
Ask about mood changes and suicidal thoughts on interleukin-17 blockers.
hold: Stop the infusion and call for wheezing, urticaria, facial swelling, or hypotension.

For interleukin inhibitors and other immunomodulating biologics, hold and call for fever, chills, or suspected active infection; do not withhold immune globulin products for infection or an infusion-related fever without provider direction.
Hold and call for a positive TB screen before the next dose.
Hold and call for new or worsening bloody diarrhea or abdominal pain.
Hold and call for urine output under 30 mL/hr or rising creatinine.
safety: Keep epinephrine, oxygen, and emergency equipment at the bedside during infusion.
Start the infusion at the ordered rate and titrate only per the order.
Hydrate before and after immune globulin unless fluid restricted; protects the kidneys.
Refrigerate biologics; warm prefilled syringes to room temperature 30 minutes before injecting.
Do not shake vials; roll gently and inspect for particles or discoloration.
Rotate subcutaneous sites and avoid plaques, bruises, scars, and the navel area.
evaluate: Confirm plaque psoriasis clears and joint pain and swelling decrease.
Confirm hemoglobin rises and LDH falls on complement inhibitors.
Confirm infection frequency does not increase over the course of therapy.
Confirm serum IgG trough stays in the ordered range on replacement therapy.

before: Check blood glucose before the dose and know the ordered target range.
Draw baseline A1C, creatinine, and eGFR.
Ask about sulfa allergy before giving a sulfonylurea.
Draw baseline liver enzymes; several agents are hepatotoxic.
Confirm the patient is eating and the meal tray is coming.
