during: Check fingerstick glucose before meals and at bedtime, or per the ordered schedule.
Watch for shakiness, sweating, tachycardia, and confusion; hypoglycemia.
Weigh daily and check ankles for edema on thiazolidinediones.
Ask about severe abdominal pain radiating to the back; pancreatitis.
Recheck A1C every 3 months to gauge control.
hold: Hold and call for blood glucose under 70 mg/dL; treat the hypoglycemia first.
Hold when the patient is NPO or the meal is skipped.
Hold and call for severe abdominal pain with vomiting; suspected pancreatitis.

On a thiazolidinedione (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone), hold and call for new dyspnea, edema, or weight gain of 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week — fluid retention can precipitate heart failure. Other oral antidiabetics do not share this effect.
Hold and call for eGFR falling below the ordered threshold.
safety: Give sulfonylureas and meglitinides with the meal, not before an unconfirmed tray.
Give acarbose and miglitol with the first bite of each meal.
Keep 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate at the bedside for hypoglycemia.
Give metformin with food to reduce nausea and diarrhea.
Teach that illness, skipped meals, and alcohol all raise hypoglycemia risk.
Teach sick-day rules: check glucose more often and call rather than stop eating.
evaluate: Confirm A1C falls toward the ordered target.
Confirm premeal glucose stays in the ordered range.
Confirm no severe hypoglycemic episodes occur.
Confirm the patient can state hypoglycemia symptoms and the 15-15 rule.

before: Obtain a 12-lead ECG and record the baseline QTc.
Check potassium and magnesium; correct low levels before dosing.
Take an apical pulse for a full minute and a baseline blood pressure.
Draw baseline creatinine and liver enzymes; most need renal or hepatic dosing.
Verify drug, dose, concentration, and pump rate with a second nurse; all are high-alert.
during: Keep continuous cardiac monitoring throughout IV therapy.
Measure QTc and QRS width on each ECG; widening signals proarrhythmia.
Take blood pressure every 5 to 15 minutes during IV loading, per policy.
Ask about dizziness, palpitations, and syncope every shift.
Recheck potassium, magnesium, and renal function during therapy.
hold: Hold and call for apical heart rate under 60 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for SBP under 90 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for QTc above the ordered threshold or any run of torsades.
Hold and call for new second- or third-degree heart block.
Hold and call for potassium or magnesium below the ordered range.
safety: Keep a defibrillator, pacing capability, and emergency drugs at the bedside.
Give IV infusions on a programmed pump; never free-flow these drugs.
Check the profile for other QT-prolonging drugs before giving a dose.
Teach the patient to rise slowly and to report fainting at once.
Have the patient take an oral pulse daily and record it before dosing.
Do not stop an oral antiarrhythmic abruptly; rebound arrhythmia can follow.
evaluate: Confirm the rhythm converts or the ventricular rate falls into the ordered range.
Confirm palpitations, dizziness, and chest pain resolve.
Confirm blood pressure and peripheral perfusion stay adequate after conversion.
Confirm drug levels stay therapeutic where levels are drawn.

before: Rate pain on a 0 to 10 scale and record the patient's goal.
Ask about ulcer disease, GI bleeding, aspirin allergy, and asthma with nasal polyps.
Draw baseline creatinine, BUN, hemoglobin, and liver enzymes.

Add up acetaminophen from every source. The maximum for a healthy adult is 4 g/day (OTC labelling advises 3 g/day); reduce to 2 g/day or less with chronic alcohol use, liver disease, malnutrition, or low body weight, and confirm the patient-specific ceiling with the provider.
Check for anticoagulants, antiplatelets, and corticosteroids on the profile.
during: Reassess pain 30 to 60 minutes after the dose and document the score.
Watch for black tarry stools, coffee-ground emesis, and epigastric pain.
Track creatinine, urine output, weight, and new edema.
Watch for chest pain, dyspnea, and slurred speech; NSAIDs raise MI and stroke risk.
Recheck temperature to confirm the antipyretic effect.
hold: Hold and call for any GI bleeding sign or a falling hemoglobin.
Hold and call for urine output under 30 mL/hr or a rising creatinine.
Hold and call for rash, wheezing, or facial swelling after a dose.

Hold when the total daily acetaminophen from all sources would exceed the patient-specific ceiling - 4 g/day for a healthy adult, but 2 g/day or less with liver disease, chronic alcohol use, malnutrition, or low body weight.
Hold and call before surgery or when active bleeding is present.
safety: Give oral NSAIDs with food, milk, or a full glass of water.
Never give two NSAIDs together; aspirin plus another NSAID is duplicate therapy.
Check every combination product for hidden acetaminophen before giving another dose.
Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester and after coronary bypass surgery.
Give IV acetaminophen over 15 minutes and verify the dose in milligrams.
Teach that these drugs mask fever, so temperature alone can miss infection.
evaluate: Confirm the pain score drops to the patient's stated goal.
Confirm fever comes down and the patient rests more comfortably.
Confirm joint swelling, stiffness, and range of motion improve.
Confirm stools stay negative for blood and creatinine stays stable.

before: Draw ordered cultures before the first dose.
Ask about macrolide or tetracycline allergy and any prior C. difficile infection.
Obtain a baseline ECG in patients at risk for QT prolongation.
Ask about pregnancy and check the age; tetracyclines are avoided under 8 years.
Draw baseline liver enzymes and creatinine.
during: Track temperature, white count, and the infection site each shift.
Watch for new watery diarrhea with fever and cramping; C. difficile.
Watch the ECG for QT prolongation on macrolides.
Track liver enzymes and bilirubin; both classes are hepatotoxic.
Ask about sunburn after brief sun exposure; photosensitivity.
hold: Hold and call for three or more watery stools with fever or abdominal pain.
Hold and call for QTc above the ordered threshold, syncope, or palpitations.
Hold and call for rash, wheezing, or facial swelling after a dose.
Hold and call for jaundice or liver enzymes above the ordered threshold.
Hold and call for severe headache with blurred vision; intracranial hypertension.
safety: Give tetracyclines with a full glass of water and stay upright 30 minutes.
Separate tetracyclines from dairy, antacids, iron, and calcium by 2 hours.
Teach sunscreen, hat, and long sleeves for the entire course.
Discard expired tetracycline; degraded drug damages the kidneys.
Screen the profile for statins, warfarin, and digoxin before a macrolide.
Teach the patient to finish the full course even after symptoms clear.
evaluate: Confirm fever resolves and the white count returns to normal.
Confirm cough, sputum, or wound drainage clears.
Confirm follow-up cultures are negative.
Confirm no diarrhea develops during or in the weeks after the course.

before: Take baseline height, weight, blood pressure, pulse, and usual sleep pattern.
Ask about cardiac disease, structural defects, and family history of sudden death.
Screen for substance use; most of these drugs are Schedule II controlled.
Ask about tics, anxiety, psychosis, and glaucoma before the first dose.
Confirm the indication; ADHD, narcolepsy, and weight agents are not interchangeable.
during: Take blood pressure and pulse at every visit and after each dose change.
Weigh weekly and plot growth in children; appetite suppression is expected.
Ask about sleep onset and total hours slept.
Watch for chest pain, palpitations, and new shortness of breath.
Ask about new agitation, hallucinations, or manic behavior.
Inspect the skin for rash; severe skin reactions occur with several agents.
hold: Hold and call for chest pain, syncope, or a new irregular rhythm.
Hold and call for blood pressure or heart rate above the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for any spreading rash, blistering, or mucosal lesions.
Hold and call for new hallucinations, aggression, or suicidal thoughts.
Hold and call when weight or growth falls below the ordered limit.
safety: Give the last dose before mid-afternoon; later doses cause insomnia.
Count and document controlled doses with a second nurse per policy.
Swallow extended-release forms whole; do not crush or chew.
Avoid caffeine and other stimulants; the cardiovascular effects add up.
Teach secure storage at home; these drugs are frequently diverted.
Give with or after food to reduce anorexia and stomach upset.
evaluate: Confirm attention, task completion, and behavior improve at school or work.
Confirm daytime sleepiness decreases on narcolepsy agents.
Confirm weight and growth stay on the expected curve.
Confirm blood pressure and pulse stay within the ordered parameters.

before: Draw baseline serum uric acid, creatinine, eGFR, CBC, and liver enzymes.
Ask about sulfa allergy before probenecid.
Assess the affected joint for swelling, redness, warmth, and range of motion.
Confirm whether the order treats an acute attack or lowers uric acid long term.
Screen for G6PD deficiency before rasburicase or pegloticase.
during: Track serum uric acid on the ordered schedule.
Track creatinine and urine output and encourage fluids each shift.
Inspect the skin at every visit; rash can precede a severe reaction.
Ask about nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea on colchicine; these are early toxicity.
Recheck CBC for agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and aplastic anemia.
hold: Stop and call for any rash on allopurinol or febuxostat.
Hold and call for diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal pain on colchicine.
Stop the infusion and call for chest pain, wheezing, or hypotension.
Hold and call for urine output under 30 mL/hr or a rising creatinine.
Hold and call for new chest pain or stroke symptoms on febuxostat.
safety: Push fluids to 2 to 3 liters daily unless restricted; prevents urate stones.
Keep epinephrine and emergency equipment at the bedside during urate oxidase infusions.
Do not start or stop urate-lowering therapy during an acute attack without an order.
Check the colchicine dose against renal function and interacting drugs.
Teach avoidance of alcohol, organ meats, shellfish, and sardines.
Elevate and rest the joint; keep bed linens off the painful toe.
evaluate: Confirm serum uric acid falls to the ordered target.
Confirm joint pain, swelling, and redness resolve within days of an acute attack.
Confirm the number of attacks per year drops over time.
Confirm creatinine stays stable and no kidney stones form.

before: Draw baseline TSH and free T4, plus T3 when ordered.
Take baseline weight, apical pulse, and blood pressure.
Ask about cardiac disease; thyroid hormone raises myocardial oxygen demand.
Draw a baseline CBC and liver enzymes before an antithyroid drug.
Ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding; the drug choice changes.
during: Take an apical pulse before each dose of thyroid hormone.
Recheck TSH and free T4 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change.
Weigh daily and track appetite, energy, and heat or cold intolerance.
Watch for chest pain, palpitations, tremor, and insomnia; overreplacement.
Ask about sore throat, fever, and mouth ulcers on antithyroid drugs.
hold: Hold and call for an apical pulse over 100 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold and call for chest pain, palpitations, or a new dysrhythmia.
Hold and call for fever, sore throat, or mouth sores; possible agranulocytosis.
Hold and call for jaundice, dark urine, or right upper quadrant pain.

Call the provider immediately for high fever with agitation and tachycardia - thyroid storm is a medical emergency. Hold levothyroxine or liothyronine and expect them to be stopped; do NOT withhold methimazole or PTU, which are part of the treatment.
safety: Give levothyroxine on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast.
Separate thyroid hormone from calcium, iron, and antacids by 4 hours.
Do not switch brands or products without a new order; potency differs.
Teach that replacement is lifelong; do not stop when feeling well.
Start low and titrate slowly in older adults and cardiac patients.
Keep the room cool and change linens often while the patient is hyperthyroid.
evaluate: Confirm TSH returns to the ordered range.
Confirm energy, weight, bowel pattern, and temperature tolerance normalize.
Confirm the resting pulse stays within the ordered parameters.
Confirm tremor, heat intolerance, and goiter size decrease on antithyroid therapy.

before: Screen for latent TB with a skin test or IGRA before the first dose.
Check hepatitis B and C serology before starting; reactivation is a boxed warning.
Draw baseline CBC with differential, LFTs, and serum creatinine.
Ask about fever, cough, open wounds, or any active infection before dosing.
Confirm needed live vaccines are done and document pregnancy status.
during: Recheck CBC and LFTs at the ordered interval; watch for a falling WBC.
Take temperature every shift; low-grade fever may be the only sign of infection.
Watch for new cough, night sweats, or weight loss suggesting reactivated TB.
Inspect skin at each visit for new or changing lesions.
Check blood pressure and weight; hypertension and edema are common.
Report leg swelling, chest pain, or dyspnea on JAK inhibitors; thrombosis risk.
hold: Report fever, chills, or suspected active infection to the provider immediately. Methotrexate, other DMARDs, and biologics are usually held during active infection - but do NOT withhold transplant immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, mycophenolate) without a provider order; abrupt interruption risks graft rejection.
Hold for an absolute neutrophil count below the ordered parameter and notify the provider.

Report LFTs above the ordered threshold, jaundice, or dark urine to the provider immediately and hold only if the order or protocol says to. Never withhold a transplant immunosuppressant (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, mycophenolate) without provider direction - missed doses risk rejection.
Hold and call for severe abdominal pain; GI perforation is an emergency.

Hold and call immediately for a positive pregnancy test on methotrexate, leflunomide, mycophenolate, or thalidomide-type agents. Do NOT stop transplant immunosuppressants (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, azathioprine, prednisone) - report the pregnancy to the transplant team and continue the drug until they direct otherwise.
safety: Keep the patient away from anyone with active chickenpox, measles, or shingles.
Withhold live vaccines during therapy; inactivated vaccines are acceptable.
Wear gloves for cytotoxic oral agents and do not crush or split them.
Rotate subcutaneous injection sites and refrigerate pens until the dose is due.
Keep epinephrine, antihistamine, and oxygen available for first infusions.
evaluate: Confirm less joint pain, swelling, and morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes.
Check that ESR and CRP trend down from baseline.
Confirm no rejection signs in transplant patients: fever, graft tenderness, rising creatinine.
Verify the patient completes daily activities with less fatigue.

before: Verify drug, dose, and patient with a second nurse before hanging.
Confirm baseline CBC, LFTs, and renal function are on the chart.
Take baseline vital signs and weight for dose calculation.
Verify patent IV access with blood return before starting.
Ask about prior infusion reactions and confirm ordered premedications were given.
during: Take vital signs before, during, and at the end of the infusion per protocol.
Stay at the bedside through the start of a first infusion.
Watch for fever, chills, rigors, flushing, dyspnea, and back pain.
Check the IV site hourly for swelling, redness, or leaking.
Screen for immune-mediated colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis, and pneumonitis on checkpoint inhibitors.
hold: Stop the infusion immediately for dyspnea, wheezing, hypotension, or chest tightness.
Hold and call for fever or ANC below the ordered parameter.
Hold for new or worsening cough and dyspnea suggesting pneumonitis.
Hold for severe diarrhea, bloody stools, or abdominal pain; colitis and perforation occur.
Hold checkpoint inhibitors for immune-mediated organ toxicity; expect corticosteroids to be ordered.
safety: Follow hazardous drug handling: gown, double gloves, closed-system transfer device.
Infuse alone through a dedicated line; do not mix with other drugs.
Keep epinephrine, diphenhydramine, corticosteroids, and oxygen at the bedside.
Use a programmable pump and start at the slowest ordered rate.
Discard tubing, bags, and waste in the hazardous drug container.
evaluate: Confirm imaging or tumor markers show response at the ordered follow-up.
Verify the patient finished the infusion with stable vital signs and no rash.
Check that ejection fraction stays within the ordered range on repeat echo.
Confirm blood counts recover before the next scheduled cycle.

before: Take baseline respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, and level of consciousness.
Ask about alcohol, opioids, and other CNS depressants in the last 24 hours.
Screen for sleep apnea, fall history, and pregnancy before the first dose.
Check the last dose time and confirm no duplicate sedative was given.
Record baseline anxiety, agitation, or sleep pattern to measure response against.
during: Count respirations and check oxygen saturation before and after each dose.
Score sedation with a standard sedation scale at the ordered interval.
Watch for paradoxical excitement, agitation, or confusion, especially in older adults.
Check blood pressure sitting and standing before the patient walks.
Ask about daytime drowsiness, sleepwalking, and memory gaps each visit.
hold: Hold and call the provider for a respiratory rate under 12 per minute.
Hold and call for oxygen saturation below 90 percent or new apnea.
Hold for systolic blood pressure under 90 or per the ordered parameters.
Hold for sedation the patient cannot be roused from and call rapid response.
Hold if alcohol or an opioid was taken recently and notify the provider.
safety: Keep oxygen, suction, and a bag-valve mask at the bedside for IV doses.
Raise side rails, lower the bed, and place the call light within reach.
Give hypnotics right at bedtime with 7 to 8 hours available for sleep.
Never stop long-term benzodiazepines abruptly; taper on the provider's order.
Store in the locked controlled-substance drawer and count per unit policy.
Tell the patient not to drive until the sedating effect has fully worn off.
evaluate: Confirm anxiety decreased without oversedation on the sedation scale.
Verify the patient falls asleep faster and wakes fewer times overnight.
Confirm seizure frequency dropped when the drug is used as an anticonvulsant.
Verify no falls occurred and gait stayed steady.

before: Draw baseline serum sodium, potassium, glucose, and renal function.
Record baseline weight, blood pressure, and 24-hour intake and output.
Check baseline LFTs; several agents in this group injure the liver.
Confirm pregnancy status before starting any hormone-modifying agent.
Verify drug name and concentration; several look-alike products are subcutaneous.
during: Weigh daily on the same scale and compare with intake and output.
Recheck serum sodium at the ordered interval; both low and high sodium occur.
Check fingerstick glucose; growth hormone and somatostatin analogs shift glucose.
Take blood pressure and heart rate before each dose.
Inspect injection sites for redness, nodules, and lipoatrophy.
hold: Hold and call for serum sodium outside the ordered parameters.
Hold if sodium rises faster than ordered; rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.
Hold and call for headache, confusion, or seizure suggesting acute hyponatremia.
Hold for LFTs above the ordered threshold, jaundice, or dark urine.
Hold and call for severe abdominal pain suggesting pancreatitis or gallstones.
safety: Start vasopressin receptor antagonists where sodium can be drawn frequently.
Rotate subcutaneous sites and store pens exactly as the manufacturer directs.
Follow the ordered fluid restriction or free water access precisely.
Keep epinephrine and anaphylaxis supplies available for first injectable doses.
Time doses around food and interacting drugs exactly as ordered.
evaluate: Confirm serum sodium sits in the target range without overcorrection.
Verify urine output and thirst normalized in diabetes insipidus.
Check that growth velocity or IGF-1 improved at the ordered follow-up.
Confirm the specific weight, symptom, or lab target was met.

before: Auscultate lung sounds and count respiratory rate before the dose.
Take baseline heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation.
Check peak flow or the ordered spirometry value before treatment.
Ask when the rescue inhaler was last used and how often.
Watch the patient use the inhaler or nebulizer and correct technique.
during: Reauscultate lungs and recheck oxygen saturation after the treatment.
Count apical heart rate; report a rise above the ordered parameter.
Watch for tremor, palpitations, nervousness, and headache from beta-2 stimulation.
Check potassium and glucose with frequent or continuous beta-agonist dosing.
Ask about dry mouth, urinary retention, and blurred vision with anticholinergics.
hold: For scheduled/maintenance bronchodilators, hold and call for HR above the ordered parameter or a new dysrhythmia. Never withhold a rescue bronchodilator from a patient in acute bronchospasm - give it, then report the heart rate.
